alignment.note: Greek frames the subject with article + postpositive δέ (Ὁ δέ, 'And he'); Syriac matches with the demonstrative-plus-particle ܗܘ ܕܝܢ. The Vulgate reduces this to a simple connective Et, dropping the resumptive pronoun and the adversative nuance of δέ.

The Greek aorist participle ἀποκριθείς ('answering') and the Latin respondens render the Semitic 'answered and said' formula; the Peshitta omits any equivalent of the responsive participle here, beginning directly with ܫܪܝ ('began'), a stylistic compression common to Syriac narrative.

Greek αὐτοῖς carries a raised dot (·) marking the transition to direct speech; the Vulgate represents the same boundary with a discrete colon token (illis :), whereas the Peshitta ܠܗܘܢ carries no separate punctuation marker.

Greek uses the simple negative particle μή introducing a clause of apprehension; Latin matches with ne. Syriac compounds the marker as ܕܠܡܐ (relative ܕ- + ܠܡܐ), forming a single conjunction 'lest', a typical Syriac construction for negative purpose/fear clauses.

Greek ὑμᾶς and Latin vos are independent accusative pronouns; Syriac encodes the second-plural object enclitically as the suffix -ܟܘܢ on the verb ܢܛܥܝܟܘܢ, a synthetic rendering of the same accusative object.

Greek πλανήσῃ ('lead astray') and Latin seducat agree on the sense of deception; the Syriac verb ܢܛܥܝܟܘܢ (root T-e-y, cf. Hebrew תָּעָה 'to wander/err') carries the same causative 'cause to go astray' force, with the Vulgate appending a closing colon.
